Fabric IQ Hands-on Lab

Gemeente Alphen aan den Rijn × Microsoft · Dublin, November 2026

Facilitators: Valerie van Loef & Richie Lee (Microsoft)

The big idea: why we're doing this

The challengeYour data sits in many tables and systems. But the knowledge of what it means lives in people's heads: when a request is urgent, which contractor is responsible, when something counts as a repeat request. An experienced colleague knows these things from years on the job. An AI agent only sees the tables, so it has to guess.
The answer: an ontologyAn ontology writes that knowledge down once, in business language. It describes the things you work with, how they're connected and the rules that apply. Think of it as the handbook a new colleague gets on day one: “this is how we work here”.
What that gives youPeople and AI agents now work from the same definitions. An agent can answer “which requests are urgent?” the way your organisation means it. Another agent can then act on that answer. Build it once, then use it everywhere.

Fabric IQ is the part of Microsoft Fabric where this happens. It connects your data to the meaning behind it, so that people and AI agents understand your organisation in the same way. The ontology is at its heart.

Today at a glance

We use a scenario that will feel familiar: service requests (meldingen) about objects in public space, the work orders that deal with them, the contractors who do the work and the neighbourhoods where it all happens. In one session you'll go from raw data to agents that answer questions and take action. No programming needed: the code is ready for you, and you work in natural language, in Dutch if you like.

Throughout the session, we work towards one question: which requests are urgent, and who needs to know?

Before you start

The easiest way to understand an ontology is to build one yourself. That's what the rest of today is about.

  1. Sign in to Microsoft Fabric and open the workspace you'll use today.
  2. Download the lab materials:
    • Notebook fabric_iq_lab_data.ipynb: Download the notebook (save it, then in your Fabric workspace choose Import > Notebook > From this computer)
    • The ontology prompt is in step 5 of this guide, ready to copy.

Your Fabric admin needs to switch on a few settings before the session. The list is at the end of this guide.

Part 1Data: bring it in

1

Create a Lakehouse Hands-on

What & whyA Lakehouse is the home for your data in Fabric. It stores data as tables that every Fabric tool can use: reports, notebooks, the ontology and AI agents.
How
  1. In your workspace, select + New item → Lakehouse.
  2. Give it a name and select Create.
2

Load the data with one ready-made notebook Hands-on

What & whyA notebook is a set of instructions that collects data and prepares it. We've written one notebook that does everything, so you don't need to read or change any code. It does three things:
  • Demo data: service requests, work orders, contractors and contracts. Fictional, but realistic, and the same for everyone.
  • Real open data: neighbourhoods and residents from CBS, neighbourhood borders from PDOK and lamp posts from the BGT. No sign-in needed.
  • Make it usable: it combines real and fictional data, makes sure every key is unique and writes six clean tables to your Lakehouse.
How
  1. In your workspace, select Import → Notebook → From this computer and choose fabric_iq_lab_data.ipynb.
  2. Open the notebook and connect it to your Lakehouse (in the panel on the left).
  3. Select Run all. It takes a few minutes.
  4. At the end you'll see six tables, each with 0 duplicate keys. That's your sign that the data is ready.
Good to know: if a public source can't be reached, the notebook uses demo data for that part. The lab always works.
3

Meet the data Hands-on

What & whyBefore we model anything, let's see what we have. This is the world you'll describe in the ontology.
DataWhat it is
Meldingen (service requests)Requests that come in by phone or through the website
Objecten (objects)Things in public space that a request is about, such as lamp posts (real, from the BGT)
Werkorders (work orders)The work that's planned to deal with a request
Aannemers (contractors)The companies that carry out the work
Contracten (contracts)The agreements with those contractors
Wijken (neighbourhoods)Real neighbourhood data from CBS
Real or fictional? Every table has its own source column, such as wijk_bron or melding_bron, that says Echt or Fictief. Each one has a different name on purpose. If all tables shared one column called bron, Fabric could link the tables on it by mistake.
Try it: open your Lakehouse and find a neighbourhood you know, such as Ridderveld or Hoorn.

Part 2Meaning: describe how the business works

4

Build the semantic model and its relationships Hands-on

What & whyA semantic model is the model behind Power BI reports. It knows your tables, how they link and how to calculate totals. The links matter most: every report, and later the ontology, follows them. Each link goes from many to one. Many requests are about one object, and many objects lie in one neighbourhood.
What the model doesn't know is what urgent means to you, or when a request counts as a repeat request. That's the gap the ontology fills.
How
  1. Open your Lakehouse and select New semantic model. Name it sm_meldingen, select the six tables and select Confirm.
  2. Open the model and select Manage relationships. Delete any relationship that Fabric created by itself, so you start clean.
  3. Add the five relationships below with New relationship. For each one, choose Many to one (*:1) and cross-filter direction Single.
  4. Compare your model with the drawing: five lines, no more.
  5. Ask yourself: with only this model, how would I find out which requests are urgent? Keep that question in mind. You'll ask it again in step 7.
From (many)To (one)Column on both sides
meldingobjectobject_id
objectwijkwijk_id
werkordermeldingmelding_id
werkorderaannemeraannemer_id
werkordercontractcontract_id
Watch out: never link on a column that ends in _bron. A link on a column that has the same few values in every row connects everything to everything. A data agent will then say the keys are “not unique”.
5

Build the ontology in plain language Hands-on

What & whyThe ontology describes your organisation in business terms:
  • The things you work with: a melding, a werkorder, an aannemer.
  • How they connect, with names you'd use yourself: a melding gaat over an object, an object ligt in a wijk.
  • Where the data is: each thing is linked to its table in the Lakehouse.
You don't have to build this by hand. You describe what you want and the ontology agent, an AI assistant, builds it for you.
How
  1. In your workspace, select + New item → Ontology (preview) and name it Ontologie_openbare_ruimte.
  2. Open the ontology agent and paste the prompt below.
  3. The agent first shows its plan. Check that it has six things and five connections, then let the agent build it.
  4. Check every connection. Select the line between two things. Both sides should show the same column, for example wijk_id and wijk_id for ligt in. Compare with the table and the drawing below, and delete anything extra.
  5. Refresh the ontology. Then read the connections as sentences: “a werkorder lost op a melding”. It should read like a description of how the work is organised.

Prompt for the ontology agent

Bouw een ontologie voor het beheer van de openbare ruimte op basis van de tabellen in mijn lakehouse. Maak zes entiteittypes, elk met één sleutel: - Wijk (tabel wijk, sleutel wijk_id) - Object (tabel object, sleutel object_id) - Melding (tabel melding, sleutel melding_id) - Werkorder (tabel werkorder, sleutel werkorder_id) - Aannemer (tabel aannemer, sleutel aannemer_id) - Contract (tabel contract, sleutel contract_id) Maak vijf relaties zonder mapping table, met aan beide kanten dezelfde kolom: - Object "ligt in" Wijk (wijk_id) - Melding "gaat over" Object (object_id) - Werkorder "lost op" Melding (melding_id) - Werkorder "wordt uitgevoerd door" Aannemer (aannemer_id) - Werkorder "valt onder" Contract (contract_id) Leg geen andere relaties en koppel nooit op kolommen die eindigen op _bron. Geef elk entiteittype een korte Nederlandse beschrijving. Laat eerst je plan zien.

Build an ontology with six things, each with one key, and exactly five connections, each linked on the same column on both sides. Never link on a column ending in _bron.

ConnectionFrom → ToColumn on both sides
ligt inObject → Wijkwijk_id
gaat overMelding → Objectobject_id
lost opWerkorder → Meldingmelding_id
wordt uitgevoerd doorWerkorder → Aannemeraannemer_id
valt onderWerkorder → Contractcontract_id
Good to know: you can also add or change things by hand, or select Generate from semantic model and choose sm_meldingen. Whichever way you choose, check the five connections in the same way.
6

Add business rules, in Dutch Hands-on

What & whyBusiness rules are the knowledge that usually lives in people's heads, now written down as plain sentences. Once a rule is in the ontology, every agent uses the same definition. That's what makes an ontology so powerful.
How
  1. Copy a rule below and ask the ontology agent to add it.
  2. Do the same for the second rule.

Rule 1: repeat request (herhaalmelding)

Een melding is een herhaalmelding als er op hetzelfde object een werkorder met status Gereed bestaat en de meldingsdatum maximaal 30 dagen na de einddatum van die werkorder ligt.

A request is a repeat request if a work order on the same object was completed and the request came in no more than 30 days after that work ended.

Rule 2: urgent

Een melding is urgent als de status Open is en de meldingsdatum meer dan 14 dagen geleden is.

A request is urgent if its status is Open and it came in more than 14 days ago.

Part 3Ask: get answers in plain language

7

Ask the data agent Hands-on

What & whyA data agent is an AI assistant you can ask questions in plain language. You don't need to know table names or write queries. Because it uses the ontology, it answers the way your organisation means it, including your definition of urgent.
How
  1. In your workspace, select + New item → Data agent.
  2. Select Add a data source and choose your ontology.
  3. In the agent's instructions, paste this line: Support group by in GQL. It helps the agent with “how many” questions.
  4. Ask the questions below, then try a few of your own.
AskWhat you should see
“Hoeveel meldingen zijn er deze week gemaakt?”
How many requests came in this week?		The number of requests from this week
“Wat zijn de urgente meldingen die we nu moeten aanpakken?”
Which urgent requests do we need to deal with now?		The requests that match your “urgent” rule from step 6

That second one is the question from step 4. The semantic model couldn't answer it on its own. The agent can, because the definition now lives in the ontology. That answers the first half of today's question: which requests are urgent?

Part 4Act: from insight to action

8

The operations agent Demo

What & whyThe data agent waits for you to ask. The operations agent takes action. It keeps an eye on the data and can send a notification to the right person. That answers the second half of today's question: who needs to know? One agent finds the urgent requests, and the other makes sure the right person hears about them.
Watch: we show an operations agent that uses the same ontology and sends a notification about urgent requests.

Part 5Chat: use the same knowledge anywhere

9

A chat agent in Microsoft Foundry Demo

What & whyYou build the ontology once and reuse it everywhere. Microsoft Foundry is where organisations build their own AI agents and apps. With Foundry IQ, such an agent can use your ontology as its knowledge, so it gives the same answers as the agents in Fabric.
Watch: we connect a Foundry agent to the ontology and ask: “Hoeveel open meldingen hebben we in Hoorn?” (How many open requests do we have in Hoorn?)
Screenshots: Microsoft Learn

Part 6Make it yours

10

Design an ontology for your own topic Optional

What & whyThe real value comes when you apply this to your own work. You've seen one example. Now try one of your own.
How
  1. Pick a topic you deal with a lot, for example truck traffic (vrachtwagenverkeer).
  2. Together, sketch the things, how they connect and one business rule.
  3. Ask the ontology agent to build it.
  4. If you already have data on this topic, connect the ontology to it.

We'll help you as you go. It doesn't have to be finished today. A good first version to take home is the goal.

Key takeaways

  1. Data alone isn't enough. AI also needs to know what the data means in your organisation.
  2. An ontology captures that meaning once: the things you work with, how they connect and the rules that apply.
  3. You build it in plain language, in Dutch if you like, with an AI assistant doing the heavy lifting.
  4. Agents can then answer and act using your definitions, not their own guesses.
  5. Build once, use everywhere: the same ontology works for reports, Fabric agents and agents in Microsoft Foundry.

Key terms

Microsoft FabricMicrosoft's data platform: one place to store, prepare, analyse and use your data.
Fabric IQThe part of Fabric that connects data to its business meaning, so people and AI understand it the same way.
LakehouseThe home for your data in Fabric, stored as tables.
NotebookA set of instructions that loads and prepares data. Today there's one ready-made notebook: you only click Run all.
Semantic modelThe model behind Power BI reports: tables, links and calculations.
OntologyA description of your organisation in business terms: the things you work with, how they connect and the rules that apply.
Business ruleA definition written as a sentence, such as when a request counts as urgent.
Ontology agentAn AI assistant that builds the ontology from your description.
Data agentAn AI assistant that answers questions about your data in plain language.
Operations agentAn AI assistant that keeps an eye on your data and takes action, such as sending a notification.
Microsoft Foundry / Foundry IQWhere organisations build their own AI agents. Foundry IQ lets those agents use knowledge such as your ontology.
